Exhort
egg-ZORT
v.
Latin exhortari, “to encourage strongly,” from ex- (intensive) + hortari (to urge). Renders the Greek parakaleō, “to call alongside, encourage, urge,” and protrepomai, “to turn forward, urge on.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To exhort is the warm, urgent calling-alongside of one believer by another for the strengthening of faith, the stirring of love, the recovery from sin, and the perseverance unto the end. The Greek parakaleō is its principal verb—a verb the New Testament uses also of beseeching, comforting, and consoling, all of which are facets of the same near, personal, encouraging speech of one soul to another. Exhortation is therefore neither cold rebuke nor breezy chat; it is the sustained, hope-anchored, gospel-shaped pressing of truth upon a fellow saint with the affection of a brother and the urgency of one who knows the warning passages. Hebrews 3:13 sets its discipline at its highest pastoral pitch: but exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. Exhortation is the ordinary mutual ministry by which the saints keep one another soft to the Spirit’s touch; without it, sin’s deceitfulness hardens hearts unobserved. Paul’s epistles are saturated with the verb. He exhorts the Romans by the mercies of God; he exhorts the Corinthians to be reconciled to God; he exhorts the Thessalonians to abound more and more; he charges Timothy to preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine. The exhorting gift is named among the gifts of the Spirit (he that exhorteth, on exhortation, Rom 12:8); the office of pastor includes it (holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers); and the ordinary believer is to practice it daily in the body. Exhortation differs from rebuke in tone (warmer), from comfort in direction (forward-pressing), from teaching in occasion (responsive to need), and from idle counsel in weight (anchored in the Word and the warning).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines EXHORT as to incite by words or advice; to animate or urge by arguments to a good deed or to any laudable conduct or course of action.

expand to see more

EXHORT, v.t. — 1. To incite by words or advice; to animate or urge by arguments to a good deed or to any laudable conduct or course of action. I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men (1 Tim 2:1). 2. To advise; to warn; to caution.

EXHORTATION, n. — The act of exhorting; the act of inciting to good deeds, with arguments or reasons; the form of words intended to incite and encourage.

📖 Key Scripture

Hebrews 3:13 — "But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin."

2 Timothy 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Romans 12:8 — "Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness."

1 Thessalonians 4:1 — "Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Exhortation is corrupted by the therapeutic register that has dropped the warning passages and left only encouragement—and by the harsh register that knows how to rebuke but has lost the warm, calling-alongside affection that is exhortation’s biblical mark.

expand to see more

The therapeutic register of contemporary evangelicalism has emptied exhortation of its warning side. The believer is to be encouraged constantly, affirmed at every turn, comforted in distress, and built up in self-esteem—but never pressed with the hard, urgent, today-shaped warnings that Hebrews 3:13 makes central to mutual exhortation. The deceitfulness of sin is at work in every saint, the warning says, and exhortation is the daily mutual ministry by which the body keeps itself from being hardened. Drop the warning and the verb decays into mere encouragement; pastoral oversight loses its prophetic edge; the saints, no longer pressed with today, lest any of you be hardened, drift quietly into the calcification the verse aims to prevent. The recovery is to put the warning back inside the encouragement: a warm, calling-alongside, hope-anchored pressing that includes the sober word the soul needs precisely because the deceitfulness of sin is real.

The opposite corruption is the harsh register that has retained the warning and lost the warmth. The brother knows how to rebuke but has lost the calling-alongside affection that is exhortation’s biblical mark; correction is delivered without the consolation, the warning without the come-let-me-walk-with-you, the truth without the love that makes the truth bearable. Exhortation is by definition near, personal, and affectionate: the brother who exhorts another stands beside him as Paraclete-shaped speech does, not above him as judge. Recover both: warning and warmth, urgency and affection, the truth pressed home with the love that earns its hearing. The two together are what the New Testament means by exhortation—and the church saturated with that exhortation is the church kept soft to the Spirit’s touch and persevering to the end.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parakaleō (to call alongside, encourage, urge) and protrepomai (to turn forward, urge on)—the warm, urgent, calling-alongside speech by which the saints keep one another soft to the Spirit’s touch.

expand to see more

Greek parakaleō (G3870) — to call alongside, exhort, encourage, comfort (the Paraclete verb).

Greek paraklēsis (G3874) — exhortation, encouragement, consolation (the noun).

Greek protrepomai (G4389) — to turn forward, urge on (Acts 18:27).

Greek noutheteō (G3560) — to admonish, warn (the sharper cousin verb of exhortation).

Usage

"Exhortation is warm and urgent at once—the calling-alongside affection of a brother combined with the gravity of one who knows the warning passages."

"Exhort one another daily, while it is called To day—the ordinary mutual ministry by which the saints keep one another from the deceitfulness of sin."

"Encouragement-only loses the warning; rebuke-only loses the warmth; biblical exhortation holds both, and the church is kept soft to the Spirit’s touch by it."
